title: Thomas puts hope of salvation in the cross—an image—so hope’s protestation is no weaker than sacrifice’s
source_text: XLIV. Certe in sacrificiis, & victimarum immolationibus, divinae omnipotentiae protestatio major non est, quam in actibus spei, quibus salutem nostram a Deo expectamus. Et tamen, juxta Thomam Aquinatem Scholae Romanae principem, in cruce, quae est imaginis species, ponimus spem salutis. Probat enim crucem illam in qua Christus crucifixus est, & etiam ejus effigies, Latria colendas esse; quoniam illi exhibemus Latriae cultum, in quo ponimus spem salutis. In cruce, vero, ex illius mente, ponimus spem salutis. Secundum illud quod cantat Ecclesia Romana, O crux Ave spes unica, Hoc passionis tempore, Auge piis justitiam, Reisque dona veniam.
pass_a_gloss: Certainly in sacrifices, and in the immolations of victims, the protestation of divine omnipotence is not greater than in the acts of hope, by which we expect our salvation from God. And yet, according to Thomas Aquinas, prince of the Roman School, in the cross, which is a species of image, we place the hope of salvation. For he proves that that cross on which Christ was crucified, and also its effigies, are to be cultivated with Latria; since we exhibit to it the cult of Latria, in which we place the hope of salvation. But in the cross, from his mind, we place the hope of salvation. According to that which the Roman Church sings, O cross Hail only hope, In this time of the passion, Increase justice for the pious, And grant pardon to the guilty.
pass_b_english: Hope’s claim on God is as strong a protestation as sacrifice’s.
Thomas still assigns latria to the true cross and its effigy because hope of salvation is set there—O crux Ave spes unica.

choices.why: Named prince of the Roman School on cross-latria.
